<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par71 />{{GHGterm|consecutive}} has the form {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּצֹק}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, &c., cf. {{GHGpar|69|f}}, where also other forms of {{GHGheb|text=יָצַק}} are given; {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּ֫יצֶר}} and {{GHGheb|text=יִּצֹּר}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=44|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=1|verse=5}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}), from {{GHGheb|text=יָצַר|translate=to form}}, are, however, used in the same sense. Cf. also {{GHGheb|text=אֶסֳּרֵם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=10|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּשַּׁ֫רְנָה}} (for {{GHGheb|text=וַתִּ׳}} according to {{GHGpar|47|k}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=12}}; {{GHGheb|text=לִיסֹּד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=31|verse=7}} (cf. {{GHGpar|69|n}}) and {{GHGheb|text=מוּסָּד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=16}}. This assimilation is found always with sibilants (most frequently with {{GHGheb|text=צ‍}}) except in the case of {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּקַּץ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=15}} (so ed. Mant., Ginsb., Kittel; but {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|Jabl.|Biblia Hebraica ex recensione D. E. Jablonski, Berolini, 1699.}}}}, Baer {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּקַץ}}) and in {{GHGheb|text=הֻ֫לֶּדֶת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=5}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=הוּלֶּדֶת}} verse 4), {{GHGterm|infinitive Hophʿal}} of {{GHGheb|text=יָלַד}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=נוּלְּדוּ}} {{GHGpar|69|t}}).<section end=par71 />

<section begin=par72 />{{GHGpar-heading|72|Verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} (vulgo {{GHGheb|text=ע״ו}}), ''e.g.'' {{GHGheb|text=קוּם}} to rise up. Paradigm M}}

Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Semit. Sprachwiss.}}, p. 144 ff.; {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, p. 605 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|72|a}}
'''1.''' According to {{GHGpar|67|a}} a large number of monosyllabic stems were brought into agreement with the triliteral form by a strengthening, or repetition, of the second radical, i.e. of the ''consonantal'' element in the stem. In another large class of stems the same object has been attained by strengthening the ''vocalic'' element. The ground-form used for these verbs is not, as in other cases ({{GHGpar|39|a}}), the 3rd ''sing. masc. perfect'', but always the {{GHGterm|infinitive construct}} form ({{GHGpar|39|b}}), the ''û'' of which is characteristic also of the {{GHGterm|imperative}} and of the ''imperfect indicative Qal''. These stems are consequently termed verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״ו}} or more correctly (see below) {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}.<ref>The term {{GHGheb|text=ע״ו}} was consequent on the view that the {{GHGterm|Wāw}} (or {{GHGheb|text=י}} in the case of verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״י}}) in these stems was originally consonantal. This view seemed especially to be supported by the return of the {{GHGterm|Wāw}} in {{GHGterm|Piʿēl}} ({{GHGheb|text=עִוֵּד}}, the {{GHGheb|text=ו}} usually passing into {{GHGheb|text=י}} as in {{GHGheb|text=קִיַּם}}, cf. Arabic ''qáwwămă''), and by certain forms of the {{GHGterm|absolute state}} of the nouns of such stems, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מֶ֫וֶת|translate=death}}, compared with {{GHGheb|text=מוּת|translate=to die}}. Hence in explaining the verbal forms a supposed stem ''qawam'' (in verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״י}} e.g. ''šayat'') was always assumed, and {{GHGheb|text=יָקוּם}} was referred to an original ''yaqwŭm'', the {{GHGterm|infinitive absolute}} {{GHGheb|text=קוֹם}} to original ''qawôm'', the {{GHGterm|participle passive}} {{GHGheb|text=קוּם}} to original ''qawûm''. It must, however, be admitted: (1) that forms like {{GHGheb|text=עִוֵּד}}, {{GHGheb|text=קִים}} (see m) are only to be found in the latest books, and are hence evidently secondary as compared with the pure Hebrew forms {{GHGheb|text=קוֹמֵם}}, &c.; (2) that to refer the verbal forms invariably to the stem {{GHGheb|text=קָוַם}}, leads in many cases to phonetic combinations which are essentially improbable, whereas the assumption of original ''middle-vowel'' stems renders a simple and natural explanation almost always possible. These {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} stems are therefore to be rigidly distinguished from the real {{GHGheb|text=ע״ו}} stems of the strong forms, such as {{GHGheb|text=רָוַח}}, {{GHGheb|text=גָּוַע}}, &c. (see below, gg).—As early as the eleventh century the right view with regard to {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} stems was taken by Samuel Hannagîd (cf. Bacher, ''Leben und Werke des Abulwalîd'', p. 16); recently by Böttcher (''Lehrbuch'', § 1112), and (also as to {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}} stems) especially by Müller, Stade, and Wellhausen (see above, {{GHGpar|67|a}}, note). On the other hand, the old view of {{GHGheb|text=ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=י}} as consonants has been recently revived by Philippi, Barth, M. Lambert, and especially Brockelmann (op. cit.).</ref>
